records.name: City Square Ceremonial Gathering Space

records.summary: A ceremonial gathering space within Melbourne's new City Square, co-designed by Greenshoot Consulting with Wurundjeri Elders. A central circular granite paved area has Woi-wurrung language set into the ground plane, a semi-circular granite seat etched with a diamond motif, and a rotating, lockable bronze Smoking Ceremony Dish on a stone plinth. Planting was selected in consultation with Wurundjeri Elders. The space supports formal ceremony and informal yarning.
records.why_it_matters: It shows how a ceremonial element can be added to an already resolved public realm while meeting operational constraints such as circulation, train station operations and smoke management. The lockable, rotating dish and the use of Elder-authored motifs are useful references for durable, culturally authored detailing.
records.description: The project is a ceremonial gathering place within Melbourne's new City Square, co-designed by Greenshoot Consulting with Wurundjeri Elders. It was commissioned after the square's design documentation was complete, so it had to fit into a resolved public realm. It sits centrally, keeps pedestrian movement and event flexibility, and needed endorsement from Traditional Owners, State Government, City of Melbourne and MTM. Early coordination dealt with circulation, train station operations and smoke management. The main element is a bronze Smoking Ceremony Dish on a granite plinth sourced from Country. The dish is rotating and lockable, balancing safety, durability and ceremonial expression. A manna gum leaf motif is embossed on the dish and etched into the plinth, taken from a sketch by a Wurundjeri Elder. A pattern inside the dish references the manna gum flower. Woi-wurrung language is set into a bespoke circular paving pattern that differs from the rest of the plaza. Semi-circular granite seating carries etched artwork by a Wurundjeri artist, drawing on William Barak's diamond motif. Planting was selected in consultation with Wurundjeri Elders, and interpretive signage supports public learning. The bronze is designed to patinate with use and touch. The space accommodates formal ceremony and informal yarning.
